title: Right to family life
subtitle: Serbia never examined this question on the merits. No authority — no court, no Asylum Office, no Commission — assessed what extradition means for the family.
intro: Article 8 ECHR guarantees the right to respect for private and family life. In extradition cases it requires the surrendering state to assess the specific consequences of separating a family — especially when minor children are deeply integrated into the host country. In Lagovsky's case, this assessment was never carried out at any stage of the Serbian proceedings.

family_block.title: The family facts
family_block.intro: This is not an abstract right to family. These are specific people, specific years of life in Serbia, and specific consequences that no authority has examined.

facts.label: Two minor children in Serbia
facts.text: Sons Aleksei (13) and Ilya (15) have lived in Belgrade since 2023. Both attend Serbian schools and speak Serbian. Aleksei plays basketball in a local club. Their lives are built in Serbia — not in Russia.

facts.label: Wife is the sole breadwinner
facts.text: After Lagovsky lost his job at a private company operating urban passenger transport services immediately after applying for asylum, the family survives entirely on the wife's income as a nurse. Lagovsky has had no health insurance for more than six months.

facts.label: Legal residence since 2023
facts.text: The family moved to Serbia legally in 2023 — with valid passports, formal employment and tax payments. The move was not flight: at the time of departure, Lagovsky was unaware of any criminal case.

facts.label: Extradition = family separation
facts.text: Transferring Lagovsky to Russia would immediately separate him from his two minor children and wife. The children have no basis or realistic ability to follow their father to Russia — a country where they have not lived and from which the family left for safety reasons.

echr_block.title: The ECHR standard under Article 8 in extradition cases

paras.text: In Othman (Abu Qatada) v. United Kingdom, application no. 8139/09, 2012, the ECtHR confirmed: when examining extradition requests, the surrendering state must assess not only whether formal requirements are met but also the Convention risks that transfer would entail. This includes Article 8.

In Boultif v. Switzerland, application no. 54273/00, 2001, the Court set out criteria — the "Boultif criteria" — that a state must apply when assessing interference with family life: length of residence, degree of children's integration, consequences of separation, citizenship of family members. Not one of these criteria received a single line in the Serbian decisions.

In Üner v. the Netherlands [GC], application no. 46410/99, 2006, the Grand Chamber clarified: the presence of minor children and their degree of rootedness in the country carry particular weight under Article 8. Children attending local schools, speaking the local language and integrated into local society are treated as an independent factor requiring substantive analysis.

In Jeunesse v. the Netherlands [GC], application no. 12738/10, 2014, the Grand Chamber established: where children are deeply integrated into the host country and have no meaningful ties to the state to which a parent is to be expelled, this is in itself a weighty argument against removal. The state must give this circumstance a substantive assessment.

failure_title: What Serbia failed to do: a complete gap in assessment
failure_desc: None of the questions listed below was addressed by any Serbian authority. These are not procedural oversights — they are a systemic failure to discharge a Convention obligation.

failures.title: Higher Court of Belgrade (4 July 2025)
failures.what_happened: The Higher Court of Belgrade granted the extradition request, finding formal compliance with the documentation package. The decision contains no reference to the right to family life, to the minor children, or to the consequences of family separation. The court stated expressly that its task was to check the document from Moscow, not to examine the merits or humanitarian circumstances.
failures.what_missing: No Article 8 assessment, no mention of the two minor sons, no analysis of the children's degree of integration in Serbia, no engagement with the Boultif/Üner/Jeunesse criteria.
failures.why_matters: Serbia, as a Council of Europe member state, bears Convention responsibility for the consequences of its extradition decision. Ignoring Article 8 at the judicial review stage does not eliminate that responsibility — it compounds it.

failures.title: Court of Appeal of Belgrade (14 November 2025)
failures.what_happened: The Court of Appeal upheld the first-instance decision. Neither the text nor the hearing records contain any assessment of family circumstances. The defence raised the presence of minor children and the family's integration in Serbia — the Court of Appeal resolved these arguments neither for nor against: it simply did not address them.
failures.what_missing: The Court of Appeal not only failed to conduct an Article 8 assessment but gave no explanation for the omission. A court's silence on a Convention argument is not an adequate response.
failures.why_matters: Under the ECtHR's approach (Othman, 2012), the surrendering state must assess the foreseeable Convention consequences of its decision. The Court of Appeal — the last judicial instance in the extradition chain — closed this question without an answer.

failures.title: Supreme Court of Serbia (11 February 2026)
failures.what_happened: The Supreme Court (Кзз ОК 1/2026) dismissed the defence application for review of legality. Article 8 ECHR arguments were included in the application — the Supreme Court categorised all arguments going to the substance of the case as "questions of fact" falling outside its competence. Thus, no court at any level of the Serbian judiciary examined the family circumstances.
failures.what_missing: The applicability of Article 8 ECHR is a question of law, not fact. Reclassifying a Convention argument as a factual issue is an improper avoidance of assessment.
failures.why_matters: The absence of substantive review under Article 8 at all three levels of the court system means that the extradition decision was made outside the Convention framework. This is itself a violation of Serbia's obligations under the ECHR.

failures.title: Asylum Office (23 February 2026) and Asylum Commission (23 March 2026)
failures.tag: Asylum proceedings · Article 8 mentioned but not assessed
failures.what_happened: The asylum application expressly invoked violations of Article 8 ECHR — family separation resulting from extradition, minor children in Serbia, the wife. The Asylum Office in decision no. 26-7707/25 of 23 February 2026 examined the situation only through the lens of Convention fear of persecution, without conducting a standalone analysis of Article 8 as a separate ground for protection. The Asylum Commission in decision AŽ-23/26 of 23 March 2026 fully upheld the refusal, also failing to engage with the question of family life on the merits.
failures.what_missing: Neither the Asylum Office nor the Asylum Commission applied the Boultif/Üner/Jeunesse criteria. References to the children's "integration" appear in the case file — the authorities saw them but did not assess them.
failures.why_matters: Subsidiary protection under Article 15(b) of the EU Qualification Directive expressly requires assessment of the risk of "inhuman or degrading treatment" — family separation involving minor children with no prospect of reunification qualifies as such a risk in ECtHR case law.

proportionality_block.title: The proportionality test: Serbia's failure
proportionality_block.intro: Article 8(2) ECHR permits interference with family life only if it is necessary in a democratic society and proportionate to the aim pursued. No Serbian authority carried out this test.

items.assessment: Extradition on a criminal fraud charge formally pursues a legitimate aim — ensuring criminal justice. However, the same transaction has been found lawful by Russian arbitrazh courts up to the Supreme Court. The legitimacy of an aim based on a criminal case concerning an act that courts found to be lawful is itself questionable.

The main defendants in the case received suspended sentences of 1 year and 10 months in Russia. The requested measure — extradition of a legal consultant with pre-trial detention — is disproportionate to the punishment that the requesting state itself considers sufficient for the principals. The necessity of separating the family is not established at this level of proportionality.

Two minor children who have lived in Serbia for more than three years, have no realistic ability to follow their father, and have a single working parent — these are concrete and serious consequences. No Serbian authority weighed these consequences against the purported necessity of extradition.

serbia_obligation.title: Serbia's Convention obligation
serbia_obligation.text: Russia left the Council of Europe in 2022. This means that after extradition, Lagovsky's children will lose their father without any Convention mechanism capable of remedying that situation: the ECtHR no longer has jurisdiction over Russia. It is Serbia, as the surrendering state, that bears full responsibility for the foreseeable Convention consequences of its decision. Since no Serbian authority carried out an Article 8 assessment, this obligation has not been discharged.

conclusion_title: Conclusion: a gap, not a decision
conclusion_paras: The absence of any Article 8 ECHR assessment in the decisions of all four Serbian authorities (Higher Court, Court of Appeal, Supreme Court, Asylum Commission) is not a procedural imprecision. It is a complete absence of Convention analysis where such analysis is mandatory.

Under ECtHR case law (Boultif, Üner, Jeunesse, Othman), a state cannot decide to extradite without answering the question of family consequences — especially where minor children deeply integrated into the host country are involved.

The Administrative Court of Serbia, hearing the appeal against the asylum refusal, is the last domestic instance that can still fill this gap. If it too fails to conduct an Article 8 assessment, Serbia will have decided on extradition in breach of its Convention obligations, and its exposure before the ECtHR will be both foreseeable and documented.
summary: No Serbian authority — not the Higher Court, not the Court of Appeal, not the Supreme Court, not the Asylum Office, not the Asylum Commission — examined the right to family life under Article 8 ECHR. Two minor sons, aged 13 and 15, integrated into Belgrade schools, were left entirely outside the analysis. Under ECtHR case law (Boultif, Üner, Jeunesse, Othman), this assessment is mandatory and cannot be substituted by a formal check of the extradition documentation package.
